text:
1.1 Purpose
This book documents the mathematical and statistical behavior that MethylPipeline actually implements. It is not a historical reconstruction of the first design notes, and it is not a promise about future refactors. The source of truth is the current code under packages/.
That rule has two consequences:

If the code and an older markdown document disagree, the code is canonical.
If the code uses an approximation or heuristic, the book says so explicitly instead of rewriting it into a cleaner but false theory story.

text:
1.2 What Counts As “Theory” In This Repository
The repository mixes several kinds of methodology. For publication-quality documentation it is important to separate them.








Category
Meaning in this book
Typical examples in MethylPipeline




Principled
Standard statistical or numerical methods used in a recognizable form
asymptotic Kolmogorov-Smirnov testing, Storey q-values, weighted log-likelihood classification, classical clustering algorithms


Approximate
A standard method implemented through discretization, asymptotics, or reconstruction from summaries rather than raw observations
histogram-based Mann-Whitney, grid-based ECDF overlap, effective-sample-size KS p-values


Heuristic
Engineered ranking, thresholding, or aggregation rules chosen for workflow utility rather than statistical optimality
effect-size ranking, module scoring constants, pairwise control aggregation


External-service-backed
Results depend on external databases, APIs, or stored procedures whose internal logic is not fully versioned inside this repository
Enrichr, DisGeNET, Open Targets, Azure SQL stored procedures, LLM-assisted evidence synthesis



That taxonomy is used throughout the book so the reader can tell where the pipeline is closest to a classical statistical method and where it is best interpreted as a reproducible engineering decision.

title: MethylPipeline: Theory, Workflows, and Reference
text:
1.4 Shared Data Model
At the lowest level the code works with per-position methylated and unmethylated counts. For a sample \(s\) at genomic position \(i\),
\[
x_{si} = \frac{m_{si}}{m_{si} + u_{si}},
\]
where \(m_{si}\) is the methylated count and \(u_{si}\) is the unmethylated count. The code clips or guards zero-coverage positions instead of leaving them undefined.
For a centroid with \(N_i\) contributing samples at locus \(i\), the shared sufficient statistics are
\[
N_i = \sum_s 1,\qquad
S_{x,i} = \sum_s x_{si},\qquad
S_{x^2,i} = \sum_s x_{si}^2.
\]
These yield the implemented centroid mean and unbiased sample variance:
\[
\hat\mu_i = \frac{S_{x,i}}{N_i},
\qquad
\hat\sigma_i^2 = \max\!\left(
\frac{S_{x^2,i} - S_{x,i}^2 / N_i}{\max(N_i - 1, 1)},
\varepsilon
\right),
\]
with a small numerical floor \(\varepsilon\) used throughout the code to avoid degenerate densities or divisions by zero.
In the ECDF-centered path, each locus also stores a binned histogram
\[
\{c_{ib}\}_{b=1}^B
\]
over shared methylation bin edges \(0 = e_0 < e_1 < \cdots < e_B = 1\). Those histograms drive both empirical distribution reconstruction and approximate rank-based testing.

title: MethylPipeline: Theory, Workflows, and Reference
text:
1.6 Cross-Cutting Assumptions
Several assumptions recur across the repository:

Loci are treated as conditionally independent inside the classifier score, even though methylation along the genome is correlated.
Multiple-testing corrections are applied across many dependent loci and, downstream, across aggregated genes. This is standard practice but should not be oversold as exact finite-sample control.
Some packages operate on summaries rather than raw per-read data. That preserves scalability, but it changes the interpretation of rank tests and distribution overlap.
Downstream packages use external services and curated priors. Those are part of the workflow, but they are not internal statistical estimators.

text:
1.7 Reading This Book
This book is organized into four parts.
Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations covers the algorithms and estimators in order from the lowest shared layer to the downstream applications. Readers interested in the production classifier should start with Chapter 2, then continue through Chapter 3, Chapter 4, and Chapter 5. Readers interested in biological interpretation should continue to Chapter 7 and Chapter 8. Chapter 10 is intentionally blunt and should be read before any publication claim is finalized.
Part II: Workflows and Production describes the two end-to-end operational workflows supported by MethylPipeline: Model Creation (repeated validation, stability analysis, production freeze, optional progression synthesis, and final --model step) and Model Use for Prediction (predictor-only evaluation of a frozen model). It also documents the project configuration file as the single source of truth for the entire pipeline.
Part III: Configuration Reference provides exhaustive tables of every parameter in every step_config section, with types, defaults, constraints, and descriptions. It is a reference, not a tutorial.
Part IV: User Guide provides step-by-step commands, output directory layout, result interpretation, and a diagnostics section covering the three most common failure modes observed in practice: low DMP coverage, class imbalance, and model version mismatch.

title: 2  MethylUtils
text:
2.3 Centroid Sufficient Statistics
For each locus \(i\), the builder stores per-sample methylation fractions \(x_{si}\) together with aggregate statistics:
\[
\hat\mu_i = \frac{S_{x,i}}{N_i},
\qquad
\hat\sigma_i^2 = \max\!\left(
\frac{S_{x^2,i} - S_{x,i}^2 / N_i}{\max(N_i - 1, 1)},
\varepsilon
\right),
\tag{2.1}\]
where \(N_i\) is the number of samples contributing to that locus and \(\varepsilon\) is a small numerical floor.
The centroid builder also stores count-level summaries:
\[
S_{m,i} = \sum_s m_{si},\qquad
S_{u,i} = \sum_s u_{si},\qquad
S_{c^2,i} = \sum_s (m_{si}+u_{si})^2,\qquad
S_{wx^2,i} = \sum_s \frac{m_{si}^2}{m_{si}+u_{si}},
\tag{2.2}\]
which are later reused by the heterogeneity calculation. Finally, each locus accumulates histogram counts \(c_{ib}\) over shared bin edges \(\{e_b\}\), producing the binned_stats object that drives both ECDF reconstruction and histogram-based testing.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 2  MethylUtils
text:
2.4 ECDF Reconstruction
The code constructs a cumulative distribution at bin edges by normalizing cumulative bin counts:
\[
\tilde F_i(e_b) =
\frac{\sum_{r \le b} c_{ir}}{\sum_{r=1}^{B} c_{ir}},
\qquad b = 0,\dots,B.
\tag{2.3}\]
ECDFView then interpolates these edge values with a monotone PCHIP spline (Fritsch and Carlson 1980). The resulting representation supplies:

a continuous cumulative distribution \(\tilde F_i(x)\),
a continuous density proxy \(\tilde f_i(x) = \max(\partial_x \tilde F_i(x), \varepsilon)\), and
numerically stable means and variances via the stored sufficient statistics.

This is an empirical-distribution model, not a beta or Gaussian fit. That distinction is central to the detector-classifier path.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 2  MethylUtils
text:
2.5 Two-Sample Comparison

2.5.1 KS Statistic on Reconstructed ECDFs
For aligned centroid pairs, the code evaluates the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic
\[
D_i = \sup_{x \in [0,1]} \left| \tilde F_{1i}(x) - \tilde F_{2i}(x) \right|.
\tag{2.4}\]
Implementation detail matters here: the supremum is approximated on a uniform grid rather than computed analytically, and the \(p\)-value is obtained from the large-sample Smirnov distribution (Kolmogorov 1933; Feller 1948) using the harmonic mean effective sample size
\[
n_{\text{eff},i} =
\frac{2}{1/\max(n_{1i},1) + 1/\max(n_{2i},1)},
\qquad
p_i = \Pr\!\left(K \ge \sqrt{n_{\text{eff},i}}\,D_i\right).
\tag{2.5}\]
This is a reasonable screening approximation, but it is not an exact finite-sample KS test on raw observations.


2.5.2 Mann-Whitney from Histogram Counts
The repository also implements a vectorized Mann-Whitney calculation directly from centroid histograms. Let \(c^{(1)}_{ib}\) and \(c^{(2)}_{ib}\) be the two groups’ bin counts at locus \(i\). The code reconstructs the \(U\) statistic as
\[
U_i =
\sum_{b=1}^{B}
c^{(1)}_{ib}
\left(
\sum_{r < b} c^{(2)}_{ir}
+ \frac{1}{2} c^{(2)}_{ib}
\right).
\tag{2.6}\]
This is followed by the usual normal approximation,
\[
\mu_{U,i} = \frac{n_{1i} n_{2i}}{2},
\qquad
Z_i = \frac{U_i - \mu_{U,i}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U_i)}},
\]
with a tie correction derived from the combined histogram counts. The important caveat is that the code does not reconstruct the full rank ordering of raw methylation values; it reconstructs a rank-like summary from histogram bins. In this book that is treated as an approximation to the classical Mann-Whitney test (Mann and Whitney 1947), not as an identical procedure.


2.5.3 Heterogeneity
dl_heterogeneity() adapts the DerSimonian-Laird method-of-moments estimator (DerSimonian and Laird 1986) to the centroid summaries:
\[
\theta_i = \frac{S_{m,i}}{S_{m,i} + S_{u,i}},
\qquad
Q_i = S_{wx^2,i} - \frac{S_{m,i}^2}{S_{m,i} + S_{u,i}},
\]
\[
\tau_i^2 =
\max\!\left(
0,\,
\frac{Q_i - \max(N_i - 1, 0)}
{\max\!\left((S_{m,i}+S_{u,i}) - S_{c^2,i}/(S_{m,i}+S_{u,i}), \varepsilon\right)}
\right).
\tag{2.7}\]
This is a useful heterogeneity diagnostic, but it should be described as a method-of-moments adaptation to stored centroid summaries, not as a full random-effects model fit.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 2  MethylUtils
text:
2.6 Continuous Overlap
Once densities have been reconstructed, the code measures shared support through
\[
O_i = \int_0^1 \min\!\left(\tilde f_{1i}(x), \tilde f_{2i}(x)\right)\,dx.
\tag{2.8}\]
Numerically, the integral is evaluated on a dense grid after each density is renormalized by trapezoidal integration. This makes the overlap robust to small interpolation drift, but it remains a grid approximation.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 2  MethylUtils
text:
2.7 Multiple Testing and p-Value Aggregation
For genome-wide DMP screening, storey_qvalues() estimates the null fraction \(\pi_0\) across a grid of \(\lambda\) values and then computes monotone q-values (Storey 2003):
\[
\hat\pi_0(\lambda) =
\frac{\#\{p_j > \lambda\}}{(1-\lambda)m},
\qquad
\hat\pi_0 = \min\!\left(1, \operatorname{median}_{\lambda} \hat\pi_0(\lambda)\right),
\]
\[
q_{(i)} = \min_{j \ge i} \frac{\hat\pi_0\,m\,p_{(j)}}{j}.
\tag{2.9}\]
The same module also provides Fisher (Fisher 1925) and Stouffer (Stouffer et al. 1949) style p-value combination utilities. Those are not central to the detector itself, but downstream packages reuse them conceptually for gene-level aggregation.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 2  MethylUtils
text:
2.8 Canonical Biological Effect Size
The repository separates statistical significance from a biological ranking score. The implemented canonical effect size is
\[
\operatorname{effect}_i =
|\Delta\mu_i|\,
(1 - O_i)\,
\exp\!\left[-\lambda_{\mathrm{var}}
\left(\sqrt{\sigma_{1i}^2} + \sqrt{\sigma_{2i}^2}\right)\right].
\tag{2.10}\]
An optional mean-level weight \(g(\bar\mu_i)\) can be applied, with the code supporting square-root, linear, saturating, and boundary-threshold variants.
This score is useful operationally, but it is not a test statistic, likelihood ratio, or posterior quantity. It is a deliberately engineered ranking rule. Publication text should therefore describe it as a heuristic biological prioritization score.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 2  MethylUtils
text:
2.9 ECDFClassifier
The classifier in ecdf_classifier.py turns the centroid histograms into per-class densities and scores a sample \(x = (x_1,\dots,x_p)\) via a weighted mean log-density:
\[
\operatorname{score}_k(x) =
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{p} w_i \log f_{ki}(x_i)}
{\sum_{i=1}^{p} w_i}.
\tag{2.11}\]
The class probabilities are then computed by temperature-scaled softmax:
\[
P(Y = k \mid x)
\propto
\exp\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{score}_k(x)}{T_{\text{eff}}}\right),
\qquad
T_{\text{eff}} = T \sqrt{n_{\text{effective}}},
\tag{2.12}\]
where \(n_{\text{effective}} = (\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2\) is the inverse-Simpson effective number of weighted loci.
Two stabilizers are important because they materially affect behavior:

log-densities are floored before averaging, so extremely small density values cannot dominate the score, and
unavailable loci are removed from the denominator by setting their effective weights to zero.

The result is a practical Naive Bayes style classifier (Domingos and Pazzani 1997), but it is not a fully calibrated generative posterior unless the independence and density assumptions actually hold. Optional Platt scaling (Platt 1999) may further recalibrate the binary probabilities after the ECDF score has been computed.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 2  MethylUtils
text:
2.10 Auxiliary Beta-Based Metrics
metrics_core.py still contains exact beta divergences, beta overlap surrogates, and moment calculations. The repository also contains a legacy beta-comparator module (methyl_utils/comparison.py). These are mathematically legitimate utilities, but they are not the main production path for DMP detection plus classification and are not used by the active detector/classifier runtime flow. In publication text, beta distances should therefore be described as an auxiliary branch of the repository, not as the canonical detector-classifier model.

title: 3  MethylCentroid
text:
3.2 What A Centroid Stores
Each persisted centroid contains:

genomic positions,
context metadata,
the sufficient statistics \(N_i\), \(S_{x,i}\), \(S_{x^2,i}\),
count summaries \(S_{m,i}\), \(S_{u,i}\), \(S_{c^2,i}\), \(S_{wx^2,i}\), and
per-locus histogram counts used to reconstruct ECDFs.

That is why the centroid is more than a mean profile. It is a compressed empirical-distribution object designed to support both detector-side testing and classifier-side scoring.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 3  MethylCentroid
text:
3.3 Sample-To-Centroid Update Rule
Given one sample with per-locus methylation fraction
\[
x_{si} = \frac{m_{si}}{m_{si} + u_{si}},
\]
the centroid builder updates
\[
N_i \leftarrow N_i + 1,\qquad
S_{x,i} \leftarrow S_{x,i} + x_{si},\qquad
S_{x^2,i} \leftarrow S_{x^2,i} + x_{si}^2.
\tag{3.1}\]
It also updates the count-derived quantities
\[
S_{m,i} \leftarrow S_{m,i} + m_{si},\qquad
S_{u,i} \leftarrow S_{u,i} + u_{si},
\]
\[
S_{c^2,i} \leftarrow S_{c^2,i} + (m_{si} + u_{si})^2,\qquad
S_{wx^2,i} \leftarrow S_{wx^2,i} + \frac{m_{si}^2}{m_{si}+u_{si}},
\tag{3.2}\]
and increments the appropriate methylation histogram bin for \(x_{si}\).
These updates make the centroid a compact empirical summary rather than a full sample-by-locus matrix.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 3  MethylCentroid
text:
3.4 Coverage Capping By Binomial Thinning
One of the most important preprocessing choices in this package is optional coverage capping. The code implements binomial thinning:

for any locus with coverage \(n_i = m_i + u_i > n_{\text{cap}}\),
compute \(p_i = n_{\text{cap}} / n_i\),
draw

\[
m_i' \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(m_i, p_i),
\qquad
u_i' \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(u_i, p_i).
\tag{3.3}\]
This preserves the methylation fraction in expectation while reducing the influence of ultra-deep loci. In other words, it is a variance-control and robustness device, not a biological model.
The implementation exposes both manual capping and auto-capping heuristics. The thinning itself is principled; the choice of \(n_{\text{cap}}\) is still a workflow decision.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 3  MethylCentroid
text:
3.5 Auto-Cap Heuristic
The package documentation describes automatic coverage capping through IQR-style heuristics computed from sampled positions. That should be interpreted as an engineering rule:
\[
n_{\text{cap}} \approx Q_3 + k\cdot \operatorname{IQR},
\]
with implementation-specific sampling and fallbacks. This is useful operationally, but it is not a statistically identified parameter.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 3  MethylCentroid
text:
3.6 Why Histograms Matter
The centroid builder stores histogram counts even though the mean and variance are already available. That is because the downstream detector and classifier do not rely only on moments. They reconstruct empirical distributions from the binned counts and then use those reconstructed distributions for overlap calculations, KS testing, and classification.
This makes methylcentroid a crucial bridge package: it is the step where sample-level methylation is transformed into an empirical-distribution object that later packages can reuse without reloading the full cohort.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 3  MethylCentroid
text:
3.7 Publication Guidance
For publication text, the safest description is:

methylcentroid constructs empirical per-locus cohort summaries,
it preserves both moments and histogram information,
it optionally reduces extreme coverage through binomial thinning, and
it is upstream of all ECDF-based detector and classifier logic.

The package should not be described as fitting a parametric methylation model. It is a summary constructor for the nonparametric empirical-distribution path.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.2 Alignment And Candidate Set
The detector starts from aligned centroid pairs, typically one control centroid and one disease centroid for a given chromosome and context. The alignment step reduces both centroids to the common set of genomic positions and propagates the empirical summaries described in Chapter 2 and Chapter 3.
Let \(\mathcal{I}\) denote the set of aligned loci under consideration for one comparison.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.3 Statistical Screening
The detector supports two closely related statistical paths:

a histogram-based path through MethylCentroidPair.compare_centroids(), and
a more precise ECDF path that recomputes KS statistics directly from reconstructed empirical distributions.

In both cases the active workflow is:

compute one p-value \(p_i\) per locus \(i \in \mathcal{I}\),
adjust all p-values to q-values using Storey q-values,
keep loci satisfying the configured q-value threshold and any minimum effect thresholds.

At the theory level this is
\[
\mathcal{D}_{\text{stat}} =
\left\{ i \in \mathcal{I} : q_i \le \alpha,\ |\Delta\mu_i| \ge \delta_{\min} \right\},
\tag{4.1}\]
with the exact choice of \(\alpha\) and \(\delta_{\min}\) coming from configuration rather than mathematical derivation.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.4 Biological Ranking
Once a statistically filtered set exists, the detector ranks loci using the canonical effect score introduced in Eq. 2.10. This gives a second set of priorities that is explicitly biological or practical rather than inferential.
The central design choice is that a locus can be:

statistically strong but biologically modest,
biologically large but not significant after multiplicity correction, or
both.

The detector keeps these notions separate instead of compressing them into one scalar.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.5 Cumulative Effect Coverage
One of the package’s characteristic filters is cumulative effect-mass selection. After sorting retained loci by decreasing effect size, the detector may keep only the smallest prefix whose cumulative effect mass reaches a specified fraction \(\gamma\) of the total:
\[
\sum_{i \in S_\gamma} e_i
\ge
\gamma \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{stat}}} e_i,
\tag{4.2}\]
where \(e_i\) is the per-locus effect score.
This is a useful way to compress large DMP sets, but it is a heuristic summarization rule rather than a statistical decision boundary with a formal optimality guarantee.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.6 Context And Chromosome Granularity
The detector is designed to run at chromosome and context granularity. In practical terms this means:

each classifier artifact is tied to a specific chromosome,
contexts such as CG, CHG, and CHH can be modeled separately or together, and
any final multiclass or multi-chromosome system is assembled later by methylclassifier.

That architecture keeps detection local and composable, but it also means that downstream fusion is not part of the detector’s statistical test itself.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.7 Exported Classifier Artifacts
The detector does more than report DMPs. It also packages the information needed by the ECDF classifier:

the filtered DMP positions,
per-class centroid histograms over those positions,
directions of methylation change, and
feature weights such as effect size.

Mathematically, this means the detector defines the feature space and the feature weighting scheme for the classifier. The classifier is therefore downstream of detector choices even when its own scoring rule is fixed.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.8 Discovery versus prediction exports
Interpretation workflows (mapping DMPs to genes, pathway enrichment, comparing stages) benefit from broader, biologically coherent DMP lists. Predictive modeling benefits from smaller, stable feature sets chosen without conflating biological narrative with classification utility.
The implementation therefore supports two coordinated outputs when dmp_export_mode=dual (default in project configs):

dmps-{chrom}-discovery.csv: all biologically filtered loci after importance ranking, without the effect-size elbow used to trim the classifier panel (unless discovery_dynamic_dmp_cutoff_enabled is turned on).
dmps-{chrom}-classifier.csv: the prediction panel after the same elbow heuristic as before, or after optional validation balanced-accuracy optimization (classifier_dmp_selection=featurecuts_validation) when validation samples are configured.

The saved ECDF classifier pickle always uses the classifier panel, not the discovery table. MethylMapper and MethylEnricher should read the discovery glob (for example dmps-*-discovery.csv). Multiclass merge utilities resolve dmps-*-classifier.csv automatically when present.
For strict evaluation of a deployed classifier, feature selection must be performed inside each outer training fold (for example by running detection on fold-specific centroids, as in Monte Carlo train splits); discovery lists built on all samples may still be reported for mechanism, but they must not be the sole basis for performance claims unless that design is stated explicitly.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.9 Production Freeze Panel
In the production workflow (Chapter 12), the detector can bypass statistical and biological discovery entirely and instead operate from a fixed list of pre-selected loci. This is configured via the fixed_dmp_panel parameter in step_config.detection.
When fixed_dmp_panel is set to a path pointing at a CSV file that contains at minimum the columns chromosome and position, the _run_multi_context method short-circuits the entire discovery pipeline. No centroids are compared, no KS statistics are computed, and no biological filtering is applied. The columns context, effect_size, statistical_dmp, and biological_dmp are inferred or set to unit defaults for any that are missing from the file. The result object is constructed directly from the loaded rows, with biological_retention_rate = 1.0 and n_statistical_dmps = n_biological_dmps = n_classifier_dmps all equal to the CSV row count.
This mechanism serves the production workflow where:

DMP positions were already validated across many Monte Carlo splits (stability analysis),
only the most reliably recurring positions are retained in the stable panel, and
the final model must use exactly those positions on the full dataset without re-running discovery.

The code path is:
MethylDetector._run_multi_context()
  ↓ if config.fixed_dmp_panel is not None
  ↓ pd.read_csv(fixed_path)
  ↓ validate columns {"chromosome", "position"} ⊆ columns
  ↓ infer missing context / effect_size / flags
  ↓ export CSV + save classifier model
  ↓ return MethylDetectorResult (no discovery performed)
The exported classifier model (PKL) is identical in structure to one built through normal discovery; downstream tools (methylclassifier, methylpredictor) are unaware of whether the positions came from live detection or a fixed panel.
Theoretical note. Using a fixed panel from a previous analysis is a form of transfer. The panel was selected on a different (possibly overlapping) set of samples. The validity of downstream statistical claims depends on whether the panel samples and the inference samples are from the same population. This is an operational design choice, not a statistical guarantee; it should be stated explicitly in any publication that uses the freeze workflow.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.10 DMP Coverage in New Samples
A frequently encountered diagnostic problem is low DMP coverage in validation or prediction samples: the classifier reports that only 10–30% of DMP positions have usable observations in a given sample. The root cause is almost always a mismatch between two coverage thresholds:

min_coverage in step_config.centroid.base_config — the minimum coverage required for a locus to be considered by centroid construction and DMP detection during training.
min_sample_coverage in step_config.detection — the minimum coverage required for a locus to be usable in a new sample during classification.

If centroid construction required min_coverage = 4 but min_sample_coverage is left at its default of 10, any locus with between 4 and 9 reads in a test sample will be dropped. Since typical WGBS data is sequenced at moderate depth and coverage varies across the genome, a large fraction of the 60 000 – 200 000 DMP positions selected during training may fall in this 4–9 read range in test samples, causing the effective feature matrix to collapse to 20% of its intended size.
The observable symptom is:
sample_dmp_coverage.dmps_used_fraction_median < 0.5
in validation_metrics.json. Values below 0.3 indicate severe coverage mismatch and nearly always lead to prediction dominated by the majority class.
Recommended practice: Set min_sample_coverage equal to the centroid min_coverage used during training. In most projects this means min_sample_coverage: 4 when base_config.min_coverage: 4. A higher min_sample_coverage is appropriate only when test samples are known to be sequenced at substantially higher depth than training centroids and locus-level precision is paramount.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 4  MethylDetector
text:
4.11 Publication Guidance
The most accurate publication description is:

methyldetector performs nonparametric locus-wise screening,
applies FDR control through Storey q-values,
supplements significance with heuristic biological ranking,
and exports a reduced, weighted empirical-distribution feature set.

When the fixed_dmp_panel path is used, the package should be described as applying a pre-specified position set rather than performing novel discovery.
The package should not be described as a pure hypothesis-testing engine if the effect-coverage filters are active, because those filters are explicitly post-test prioritization rules.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.1 Role
methylclassifier is the orchestration layer that applies one or more binary ECDF classifiers to new samples. The mathematical core still lives in methyl_utils/ecdf_classifier.py, but methylclassifier determines how per-chromosome models, one-vs-rest bundles, and pairwise disease heads are fused into final probabilities.
The relevant implementation files are:
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
packages/methylclassifier/methyl_classifier/core/classifier.py
packages/methylclassifier/methyl_classifier/core/multiclass_ovr.py
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.2 Binary Classification
For a single binary model, the underlying score is the ECDF log-density average described in Eq. 2.11 and Eq. 2.12. From the perspective of methylclassifier, the main practical issues are:

aligning the input sample to the stored DMP order,
constructing an availability mask for missing loci, and
optionally applying a stored Platt calibrator.

If the binary classifier is used alone, this is the cleanest statistical story in the package.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.3 Multi-Chromosome Binary Classification
When a detector run exports one classifier per chromosome, methylclassifier computes chromosome-specific binary probabilities and then fuses them using normalized weights:
\[
\hat p(y \mid x)
\propto
\sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} w_c\,\hat p_c(y \mid x_c),
\qquad
\sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} w_c > 0.
\tag{5.1}\]
The code supports several ways to determine the weights \(w_c\):

fixed configuration weights,
trimmed mean effect-size weights derived from detector output,
fitted linear, ridge, lasso, logistic, or elastic-net models trained on validation probabilities.

The last family is best understood as a second-stage meta-model that uses per-chromosome probabilities as features. It can improve prediction, but it is no longer a single coherent generative model.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.4 One-vs-Rest (OvR) Multiclass Fusion
For multiclass problems the package builds \(K\) binary heads and fuses them into a \(K\)-class probability vector. The active implementation in multiclass_ovr.py uses binary probabilities or logits as intermediate scores and then applies a softmax-like normalization. In symbolic form,
\[
\ell_k(x) = \log \hat p_k(y = k \mid x) - \log \hat p_k(y \neq k \mid x),
\]
\[
\hat P(Y = k \mid x)
=
\frac{\exp(\ell_k(x))}
{\sum_{r=1}^{K} \exp(\ell_r(x))}.
\tag{5.2}\]
This is a practical multiclass reduction. It is not guaranteed to recover a single joint Bayesian posterior unless the binary heads are themselves perfectly compatible.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.5 Pairwise Control Aggregation
Some project layouts export only pairwise control-vs-disease detectors. In that case the package constructs the control class probability from the geometric mean of the pairwise control probabilities:
\[
\hat p_{\text{ctrl}}(x)
=
\exp\!\left(
\frac{1}{K-1}
\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}
\log \hat p_{\text{ctrl} \mid \text{ctrl-vs-}k}(x)
\right).
\tag{5.3}\]
The complement \(1 - \hat p_{\text{ctrl}}(x)\) is then used to form a binary control-vs-rest head before final row normalization.
This is a useful aggregation rule, but it is a heuristic. The geometric mean is not derived in the code from a global multiclass likelihood.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.6 Bipartite Multi-Control × Multi-Disease Aggregation
The package also supports bipartite layouts with several control strata and several disease strata. Here it aggregates one probability column across several pairwise experts, again using geometric means. The logic is similar to Eq. 5.3 but now applied to either the control column or the disease column depending on which class head is being built.
That construction is convenient for complex cohort hierarchies, but it should be presented as a carefully engineered reduction strategy rather than a textbook probabilistic model.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.7 Calibration
When enabled, the package can apply Platt scaling (Platt 1999) to the raw binary outputs. In effect, one learns parameters \(a\) and \(b\) so that a raw score \(s\) is mapped to
\[
\hat p(y=1 \mid s) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(as + b)}.
\tag{5.4}\]
This improves probability calibration under distribution shift or class imbalance, but it should not be confused with changing the underlying classifier likelihood.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.8 New Modeling Features in Production
Recent versions of methylclassifier expose a broader post-detector modeling layer than the original binary ECDF-only story. In practice, production runs may combine several of the following:

native multiclass histogram model export (multiclass-classifier.pkl) from per-comparison detector outputs,
optional learned multinomial logistic head on top of histogram pre-softmax scores,
optional isotonic calibration for probability reshaping,
optional elastic-net stacking for chromosome-level fusion,
hierarchical panel readout for family-level reporting.

These are all valid engineering extensions, but conceptually they sit on top of the ECDF likelihood core rather than replacing it.

5.8.1 Learned Multiclass Head
The learned head takes base multiclass score vectors \(z(x)\) and fits a multinomial logistic layer:
\[
\hat P(Y=k\mid x)
=
\frac{\exp(\beta_k^\top z(x)+b_k)}
{\sum_{r=1}^K \exp(\beta_r^\top z(x)+b_r)}.
\]
This layer is controlled by multiclass_train_learned_head and related hyperparameters in step_config.detection (see Chapter 13). It is especially useful when the raw histogram scores have good ranking behavior but imperfect class boundaries.


5.8.2 Isotonic and Stacking Layers
Two additional modeling switches in step_config.classifier are important for current production behavior:

use_isotonic_calibration: nonparametric monotone calibration of predicted probabilities,
use_elasticnet_stacking: linear meta-model for chromosome-weight fusion under elastic-net regularization.

Both improve empirical calibration or discrimination in many cohorts, but they increase model complexity and should be reported explicitly in methods sections.


5.8.3 Practical Reproducibility
For reproducibility claims, report:

whether the learned multiclass head was enabled,
whether class balancing was used (multiclass_learned_class_weight),
whether isotonic calibration and/or elastic-net stacking were enabled,
the sklearn version stored in PKL metadata.

Without these details, two runs with the same DMP panel can still produce materially different probabilities.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.9 Multiclass Learned Head: Class Weighting
When the native multiclass histogram classifier is extended with a learned logistic head (multiclass_train_learned_head: true), the logistic regression is fitted on top of the pre-softmax histogram scores from the base model. This second-stage model can accept a class_weight parameter (exposed as multiclass_learned_class_weight in step_config.detection; see Chapter 13).
With multiclass_learned_class_weight: "balanced", sklearn computes inverse-frequency weights:
\[
w_k = \frac{n_{\text{total}}}{K \cdot n_k},
\tag{5.5}\]
where \(n_k\) is the number of training samples in class \(k\), \(K\) is the number of classes, and \(n_{\text{total}} = \sum_k n_k\). These weights are passed to the loss function of the multinomial logistic regression, penalizing errors on minority classes more heavily.
This is particularly important for the prostate cancer staging problem where the healthy control cohort may be two to four times larger than any individual disease stage cohort. Without balancing, the logistic head learns to predict the healthy class as the default when the pre-softmax histogram scores do not provide strong class separation (for example, when only 20% of DMP positions are covered in a test sample; see Section 4.10).
Theoretical note. Class weighting corrects for imbalance in the empirical class frequencies of the training set. It does not correct for population prevalence differences between training and deployment contexts. If the intended clinical population has very different disease prevalence from the training cohort, additional calibration against the target distribution is required.
Reproducibility. Since sklearn 1.4, the version of sklearn used to train the logistic head is saved in the model PKL metadata under the key sklearn_version. This allows detection of version mismatches between training and inference environments. The key is written by _fit_learned_multiclass_head in packages/methylclassifier/methyl_classifier/utils/multiclass_builder.py.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.10 Missing Data Semantics
A practical but important detail is how the classifier handles unavailable loci. The implementation masks those loci out of the weighted average rather than imputing them with a full modeled distribution. As a result, the effective evidence for a sample depends on how many DMPs are observed for that sample.
This is a sensible engineering choice, but it means that the posterior confidence is partly a function of data availability as well as class separation.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 5  MethylClassifier
text:
5.11 Publication Guidance
The strongest defensible summary is:

the binary head is an ECDF-based Naive Bayes style score with optional calibration,
multi-chromosome fusion is a weighted ensemble,
multiclass OvR is a reduction from binary heads to a normalized \(K\)-class score,
pairwise control aggregation is heuristic,
and fitted chromosome weights are second-stage discriminative models, not part of the original density model.

That framing is more accurate than calling the entire package a single Bayesian multiclass classifier.




Platt, John C. 1999. “Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines and Comparisons to Regularized Likelihood Methods.” In Advances in Large Margin Classifiers. MIT Press.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.1 Role
methylpredictor, methylvalidation, and methyldiseaseprogression do not introduce a new generative methylation model. Instead they evaluate, operationalize, and synthesize outputs exported by detector/classifier/mapper/enricher stages.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
methylpredictor applies trained classifier artifacts to new cohorts and computes prediction summaries.
methylvalidation creates repeated train/validation splits and aggregates run-level metrics across Monte Carlo style repetitions.
methyldiseaseprogression aggregates per-comparison mapper/enricher outputs into ordered cross-stage progression tables and labels.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.2 MethylPredictor: Labeled Evaluation
When labels are available, methylpredictor computes standard classification metrics using sklearn.metrics. For \(n\) labeled samples with true labels \(y_i\) and predictions \(\hat y_i\),
\[
\operatorname{Accuracy}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{\hat y_i = y_i\},
\]
\[
\operatorname{BalancedAccuracy}
=
\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\operatorname{Recall}_k.
\tag{6.1}\]
For binary classification the package also reports:
\[
\operatorname{Sensitivity} = \operatorname{Recall}_{\text{positive}},
\qquad
\operatorname{Specificity} = \operatorname{Recall}_{\text{negative}}.
\]
For multiclass settings it reports per-class precision, recall, \(F_1\), as well as macro and weighted \(F_1\) summaries.
These are standard descriptive metrics. Their interpretation depends on how the evaluation cohort was assembled rather than on any special estimator inside the package.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.3 Blind Prediction Summaries
In blind mode, methylpredictor cannot estimate discrimination performance because no truth labels are available. Instead it reports:

predicted class counts,
mean predicted probability per class, and
mean Shannon entropy of the per-sample class probabilities.

For one sample with class probabilities \(p_1,\dots,p_K\), entropy is
\[
H(p) = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k \log p_k.
\tag{6.2}\]
Low entropy corresponds to confident predictions; high entropy corresponds to diffuse class assignments. This is an uncertainty summary, not an accuracy estimate.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.4 MethylValidation: Split Strategy
methylvalidation implements repeated train/validation splitting by cohort. For each cohort with \(n\) samples and train fraction \(\rho\), the code computes
\[
n_{\text{train}} = \max(1, \lfloor \rho n \rfloor),
\]
and then reduces \(n_{\text{train}}\) to \(n-1\) if necessary so that the validation set is non-empty for \(n > 1\).
This is called “stratified” in the code because each cohort is split separately, but it is not identical to the textbook StratifiedKFold abstraction. The package performs independent random shuffles within each cohort and then concatenates the resulting class-specific train and validation groups.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.5 Monte Carlo Evaluation
The validation package repeatedly:

generates train and validation cohorts,
writes run-specific project files,
runs the full pipeline from centroid through predictor, and
aggregates scalar metrics across repetitions.

If \(m_r\) denotes some metric from run \(r\), the package reports descriptive summaries such as
\[
\bar m = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R} m_r,
\qquad
s_m^2 = \frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(m_r - \bar m)^2,
\]
along with empirical percentiles.
This is best interpreted as repeated internal validation of the whole pipeline, not as a formal confidence interval for an external deployment population.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
section: 6.6 What The Validation Layer Does Not Do
text:
6.6 What The Validation Layer Does Not Do
The current implementation does not attempt:

nested hyperparameter tuning,
exact sampling-theory confidence intervals for each metric,
dependence-aware aggregation across repeated splits, or
external-cohort transportability analysis.

Those omissions are not flaws in themselves, but they matter for publication wording. The package measures empirical variation across repeated pipeline runs; it does not prove generalization bounds.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.7 Stability Analysis
After completing a set of Monte Carlo runs, the --stability mode aggregates DMP recurrence across runs. For each discovery DMP \(d\) (a (chromosome, position) pair), define the recurrence indicator
\[
\mathbf{1}_r(d) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } d \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{disc},r} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\mathcal{D}_{\text{disc},r}\) is the set of discovery DMPs from run \(r\). When a minimum balanced accuracy threshold \(\beta_{\min}\) is configured, only qualifying runs (those with \(\widehat{\text{BA}}_r \ge \beta_{\min}\)) contribute to the count. Let \(R^*\) denote the number of qualifying runs. The estimated recurrence frequency is
\[
\hat{f}(d) = \frac{1}{R^*} \sum_{r=1}^{R^*} \mathbf{1}_r(d).
\tag{6.3}\]
A DMP is declared stable if \(\hat{f}(d) \ge \tau\) for a user-specified threshold \(\tau\) (default 0.7, stability_dmp_freq). The output is a CSV file stable_dmps_production.csv containing all stable DMPs with their frequencies, sorted by decreasing frequency.
Gene stability is an analogous measure over enricher gene lists: the frequency at which each gene appears in enrichment results across qualifying runs.
Theoretical note. \(\hat{f}(d)\) is an empirical frequency, not a formal probability. It depends on the train fraction \(\rho\), the random seed, and the number of iterations \(R\). With small \(R\) the estimate is noisy. The threshold \(\tau\) is a heuristic engineering choice, not derived from any optimality criterion. Higher \(\tau\) produces smaller, more reproducible panels; lower \(\tau\) retains more positions at the cost of including split-dependent noise.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.8 Production Freeze
The production freeze converts the stable DMP panel into a fixed discovery/interpretable production run on the full dataset. The --freeze flag calls freeze_production_model() in packages/methylvalidation/methyl_validation/stability.py, which:

Merges one or more per-chromosome stable DMP CSVs into a single genome-wide panel (stable_dmps_genomewide.csv).
Loads the base project JSON and injects fixed_dmp_panel into step_config.detection (pointing at the merged CSV).
Writes a production/project.json with project_name = "production" and output_base routed to the production directory.
Executes run_pipeline_for_production(), which runs: methyl-centroid → methyl-detector(fixed panel) → methyl-mapper → methyl-enricher.
Optionally runs methyl-disease-progression when step_config.progression.enabled=true.
Writes a production_summary.json summarizing the run.

Final model fitting is a separate explicit step: methyl-validation --model runs methyl-classifier → methyl-predictor on production/project.json.
If configured (step_config.validation.require_biological_review_for_model=true), --model is blocked until biological_review_confirmed=true.
The production project JSON (production/project.json) is the artifact that links the frozen model to the --predictor-only workflow: it encodes the centroid directories, detection output paths, and classifier paths so that methyl-predictor can resolve them without re-running any upstream steps.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.9 Hybrid Generative Backend (model_backend=generative_hybrid)
The --model stage now supports a first-class hybrid generative backend in addition to the legacy ECDF path and the tabular sklearn path. This backend is orchestrated by methylvalidation and uses the same detector-derived DMP bundle as the other non-ECDF model backends.

6.9.1 Data Contract and Bundle Reuse
The backend does not re-derive DMP biology or feature importance. Instead it consumes the ModelFeatureBundle generated from detector exports:

DMP index (chromosome, position, context)
detector-side effect_size and weight columns
class labels resolved from project comparisons/groups

This keeps biological weighting aligned with detector outputs and avoids backend-specific feature redefinition.


6.9.2 Modeling Structure
The implemented hybrid backend follows a VAE-style latent-density pattern:

encode weighted methylation features into a latent representation \(z\) (current implementation uses a linear latent encoder surrogate),
fit class-conditional latent densities (currently diagonal Gaussian),
compute class posteriors via Bayes-style normalization.

In symbolic form, for classes \(k=1,\dots,K\):
\[
p(z \mid y=k) \approx \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_k,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_k^2)\right),
\]
\[
\hat P(y=k\mid z)
=
\frac{\pi_k\,p(z\mid y=k)}
{\sum_{r=1}^{K}\pi_r\,p(z\mid y=r)}.
\]
This yields likelihood-based scoring for both binary and multiclass settings while preserving the detector-derived feature index.


6.9.3 Orchestration in --model
When step_config.validation.model_backend="generative_hybrid", run_pipeline_for_model() executes:

model-bundle: build_model_feature_bundle(...)
generative-train: train_generative_model(...)
generative-predictor: predict_generative_model_from_project(...)

instead of the legacy methyl-classifier -> methyl-predictor ECDF chain.


6.9.4 Configuration Surface
The backend is controlled under step_config.validation:

model_backend: "generative_hybrid"
model_bundle_dir, model_weight_column
generative_latent_dim
generative_kl_weight
generative_density_type (currently diag_gaussian)
generative_epochs, generative_batch_size, generative_seed
generative_calibrate
covariates_path, covariate_id_column
generative_covariates_strict

Those fields are part of the same validation config object as Monte Carlo settings, so backend choice is fully reproducible from project JSON.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.10 MethylDiseaseProgression Synthesis
methyl-disease-progression is a post-freeze synthesis step that treats disease groups as an ordered stage sequence and aggregates entity-level signals across stages.

6.10.1 Inputs and Stage Resolution
For each ordered stage, the code reads:

mapper combined gene table (all-gene_name-combined.csv by default),
enricher pathway table (enrichment_merged.csv, fallback enrichment_top_q0.05.csv),
optional module table (modules_ranked.csv).

Stage order comes from:

CLI --ordered-comparison-labels (highest precedence),
step_config.progression.ordered_comparison_labels (or alias ordered_disease_groups),
project comparison order.



6.10.2 Entity Scores
The synthesis creates long-format tables for genes, pathways, and modules with (entity_type, entity_id, stage_index, rank, score).

Genes: score is max of available gene-weight columns per gene (e.g. total_weight, gene_importance).
Pathways: when q-values exist, score is transformed to

\[
\operatorname{score}_{\text{pathway}} = -\log_{10}(\max(q, 10^{-300})),
\]
so larger values indicate stronger enrichment. - Modules: score is the module score exported by modules_ranked.csv.


6.10.3 Progression Labels
For each entity across ordered stages, the package assigns categorical progression labels:

stage_specific, early_only, late_only,
stable_across_stages,
monotonic_up / monotonic_down (based on adjacent score differences over at least three points).

These are deterministic rule-based labels, not fitted trajectory models.


6.10.4 Outputs
The progression step writes:

genes_long.csv
pathways_long.csv
modules_long.csv
entities_progression_labels.csv
summary.json
optional report.md (when report_md=true)

This layer is best interpreted as structured biological summarization across stages, not causal disease dynamics inference.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.11 Two Workflows Summary
MethylValidation supports two primary operational modes, described in full in Chapter 12. A brief summary for theory readers:
Workflow 1 — Model Creation. Repeated Monte Carlo runs with --stability estimate DMP recurrence frequencies from centroid+detector iterations. The --freeze step then builds production biological outputs on the stable panel (fixed_dmp_panel) and may run progression synthesis. The --model step then performs final classifier/predictor execution after optional biological gate checks.
Workflow 2 — Model Use for Prediction. The --predictor-only flag evaluates the frozen production model on repeated random holdouts without retraining. This workflow answers the question: what is the empirical distribution of classification performance for the frozen production classifier under random sampling from the available cohort?
The two workflows share the same split-and-aggregate infrastructure (split.py, project_gen.py, pipeline_runner.py) but differ in which pipeline steps execute per iteration. Workflow 1 iterations run centroid+detector; Workflow 2 iterations run predictor only.

title: 6  MethylPredictor, MethylValidation, and MethylDiseaseProgression
text:
6.12 Publication Guidance
For publication text:

describe methylpredictor as the evaluation and application layer for trained classifiers,
reserve discrimination claims for labeled validation cohorts,
treat blind-mode entropy as an uncertainty diagnostic only,
describe methylvalidation as repeated split-sample internal validation of the end-to-end workflow,
report the stability threshold \(\tau\) and the number of qualifying runs \(R^*\) when using --stability, and
state explicitly whether the production model was trained on all samples or on a split-specific subset.

That is both accurate to the code and defensible statistically.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 7  MethylMapper
text:
7.1 Role
methylmapper converts locus-level detector output into gene- and region-level annotations. It has two distinct mathematical layers:
The relevant code lives primarily in:
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 7  MethylMapper
text:
deterministic genomic mapping through bedtools-style interval logic or an external Azure SQL stored procedure, and
gene-level aggregation and disease-evidence enrichment.



packages/methylmapper/methyl_mapper/bedtools_mapper.py
packages/methylmapper/methyl_mapper/mapper.py
packages/methylmapper/methyl_mapper/gene_disease_enricher.py
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 7  MethylMapper
text:
7.2 Interval Mapping
The bedtools path maps DMP coordinates to genomic features such as promoters, exons, introns, and gene bodies. This part is deterministic interval algebra rather than statistical inference. Feature-level weights may then be attached, for example promoter weights or exon weights, but those weights are biological priors chosen by the workflow rather than estimated model parameters.
The Azure SQL path calls a stored procedure (spMapDMP2Genes). Because the stored procedure logic is external to the repository, its exact mapping semantics should be documented as an external dependency rather than as a transparent in-repo algorithm.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 7  MethylMapper
text:
7.3 Gene-Level Combined p-Values
For genes with several mapped DMPs, the package computes a signed weighted Stouffer aggregation. Given DMP p-values \(p_j\), weights \(w_j\), and direction signs \(s_j \in \{-1,+1\}\),
\[
z_j = \Phi^{-1}(1 - p_j/2),
\qquad
\tilde z_j = s_j z_j,
\]
\[
Z_{\text{gene}} =
\frac{\sum_j w_j \tilde z_j}
{\sqrt{\sum_j w_j^2}},
\qquad
p_{\text{gene}} = 2\left[1-\Phi(|Z_{\text{gene}}|)\right].
\tag{7.1}\]
The package then applies Storey q-values to the resulting gene-level p-values.
This is a standard meta-analytic construction in form (Stouffer et al. 1949), but its interpretation requires care: mapped DMPs within one gene are correlated along the genome, so the independence assumption behind classical Stouffer aggregation is only approximate.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 7  MethylMapper
text:
7.4 Biological Importance Score
calculate_biological_importance() combines detector statistics such as delta_mean, overlap, and std into a bounded gene- or region-level importance score. This is not a likelihood or hypothesis test. It is an engineered prioritization score meant to rank biologically interesting genes after mapping.
Publication text should call this what it is: a heuristic importance score that mixes detector-derived quantities and feature weights.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 7  MethylMapper
text:
7.5 Stable Gene Set Optimization
The package also contains routines that choose the number of top DMPs required to obtain a stable gene set. These routines are operationally useful, but they are not estimators with standard sampling distributions. Their parameters, step sizes, and stability thresholds should therefore be documented as tuning knobs.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 7  MethylMapper
text:
7.6 External Evidence Enrichment
GeneDiseaseEnricher queries external services such as DisGeNET (Piñero et al. 2020), Open Targets (Ochoa et al. 2023), and optional Grok-mediated evidence pipelines. This is a valuable biological annotation layer, but it is not in-repo statistical inference. The final evidence depends on:

service availability,
service version,
cached responses,
threshold profiles such as strict or balanced, and
optional LLM-assisted synthesis.

For publication, that layer must be framed as external evidence gathering and summarization rather than as a mathematically identified part of the detector.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 7  MethylMapper
text:
7.7 Publication Guidance
The most defensible description is:

interval mapping is deterministic annotation,
gene-level p-values are weighted Stouffer aggregates with dependence caveats,
gene importance is heuristic,
and disease evidence is external-service-backed annotation.

That is still scientifically useful, but it is not the same kind of object as the upstream ECDF hypothesis tests.

Piñero, Janet, Juan M. Ramírez-Anguita, Judit Saüch-Pitarch, et al. 2020. “The DisGeNET Knowledge Platform for Disease Genomics: 2019 Update.” Nucleic Acids Research 48 (D1): D845–55. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkz1021.


Stouffer, Samuel A., Edward A. Suchman, Leland C. DeVinney, Shirley A. Star, and Robin M. Williams. 1949. The American Soldier: Adjustment During Army Life. Princeton University Press.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 8  MethylEnricher
text:
8.1 Role
methylenricher is a downstream interpretation layer. It takes mapped genes or weighted gene lists and organizes them into pathway-level and module-level summaries. The package mixes three kinds of methodology:
Because of that mixture, this package should be described as a discovery and prioritization layer, not as a single statistical model.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 8  MethylEnricher
text:
external enrichment analysis through Enrichr (Chen et al. 2013),
graph-based pathway grouping,
heuristic module ranking and disease-prior labeling.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 8  MethylEnricher
text:
8.2 Over-Representation Analysis
The enrichment step is delegated to Enrichr through gseapy.enrichr. In practice this means the repository submits a gene list to an external enrichment engine and then reads back adjusted p-values, odds ratios, and gene memberships for the selected libraries.
The statistical test itself therefore lives outside the repository. The in-repo code is responsible for:

choosing the input genes,
selecting the enrichment libraries,
filtering the returned tables, and
carrying forward the adjusted p-values into later scoring steps.

Publication text should cite Enrichr (Chen et al. 2013) and record the exact library set used in the analysis. In MethylEnricher this can be done either by logging an explicit libraries list or by logging a named library_preset (for example cancer-extended for cancer-focused studies).
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 8  MethylEnricher
text:
8.3 Pathway Graph Construction
The package builds a pathway graph in which nodes are pathways and edges represent gene-set overlap. In the simplest case the edge weight is based on Jaccard similarity:
\[
J(A,B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|},
\tag{8.1}\]
or a closely related overlap score. Community detection is then performed with the Louvain method (Blondel et al. 2008), with connected-components fallbacks if the required package is unavailable.
This is a standard graph heuristic for organizing pathways, but the resulting modules depend materially on the chosen threshold, graph construction rule, and Louvain resolution behavior.
When broad library presets are used (for example cancer-extended), module construction can include tens of thousands of enrichment terms. The implementation now supports pre-clustering term reduction so modules can be built from a focused subset:

q-value gate (module_cluster_max_q): keep only terms with adjusted p-value below a threshold,
per-library cap (module_cluster_top_terms_per_library): keep top N terms per library before graph construction.

These controls change the module graph itself, not only the display layer, so they should be reported in methods sections.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 8  MethylEnricher
text:
8.4 Module Enrichment Score
compute_module_enrichment_score() converts a module into a scalar ranking score by combining:

mean \(-\log_{10}(q)\) across pathways,
number of pathways,
number of genes,
mean gene weight.

In normalized form the score is
\[
\operatorname{score}_{\text{enrich}}
=
0.4\,\tilde m_{-\log_{10} q}
+ 0.2\,\tilde n_{\text{pathways}}
+ 0.2\,\tilde n_{\text{genes}}
+ 0.2\,\tilde m_{\text{gene-weight}},
\tag{8.2}\]
where each tilded quantity is clipped to \([0,1]\) after dividing by a hand-chosen scale such as \(10\), \(50\), or \(200\).
This is explicitly heuristic. It is a ranking function, not an enrichment test.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 8  MethylEnricher
text:
8.5 Disease Relevance Prior
The package also computes a disease-relevance score by overlap with a curated gene set:
\[
\operatorname{score}_{\text{disease}}
=
\frac{|G_{\text{module}} \cap G_{\text{disease}}|}
{|G_{\text{module}}|}.
\tag{8.3}\]
When no disease set is available the package returns a neutral value of \(0.5\). By default the code ships with a prostate-cancer-oriented prior gene set, so that default must not be described as disease-agnostic.
The final module score is then
\[
\operatorname{score}_{\text{final}}
=
0.7\,\operatorname{score}_{\text{enrich}}
+ 0.3\,\operatorname{score}_{\text{disease}}.
\tag{8.4}\]
This is again a heuristic prioritization rule.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 8  MethylEnricher
text:
8.6 Theme Normalization And Labels
The package includes theme normalization based on substring matching against a JSON mapping file, plus discrete labels such as High, Medium, and Low relevance. Those labels are workflow conveniences. They should not be presented as probabilistic classifications.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 8  MethylEnricher
text:
8.7 Publication Guidance
The most accurate description is:

enrichment significance comes from an external ORA engine,
pathway modules come from graph clustering over pathway overlap,
module ranking is heuristic,
and disease relevance is a curated prior overlap rather than a learned posterior.

That combination can be highly useful for interpretation, but it should be framed as an annotation and prioritization pipeline rather than as formal inference.




Blondel, Vincent D., Jean-Loup Guillaume, Renaud Lambiotte, and Etienne Lefebvre. 2008. “Fast Unfolding of Communities in Large Networks.” Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment 2008 (10): P10008. https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-5468/2008/10/P10008.


Chen, Edward Y., Christopher M. Tan, Yan Kou, et al. 2013. “Enrichr: Interactive and Collaborative HTML5 Gene List Enrichment Analysis Tool.” BMC Bioinformatics 14: 128. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2105-14-128.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 9  MethylAlignmentQC
text:
9.1 Role
methylalignmentqc is the least inferential package in the repository. It parses alignment and duplication metrics produced by external tools such as Picard and Parabricks, then rewrites them into structured JSON for downstream inspection.
The package therefore belongs in the theory book only so that readers do not over-interpret it. Its main functions are deterministic parsing, normalization, and reporting.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 9  MethylAlignmentQC
text:
9.2 Deterministic Metric Extraction
The parser reads tabular metrics files, histograms, and summary blocks and maps selected fields into a fixed schema. Typical examples include:

total reads,
duplicate counts,
duplication rate,
related read-group or library statistics.

There is no new statistical estimator here beyond whatever upstream alignment tool already computed.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 9  MethylAlignmentQC
text:
9.3 Summary Statistics
When the package computes summaries such as duplication rate, it is applying straightforward algebra:
\[
\operatorname{duplication\ rate}
=
\frac{\text{duplicate reads}}{\text{total reads}}.
\tag{9.1}\]
These are useful QC diagnostics, but they do not form a novel methylation model.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 9  MethylAlignmentQC
text:
9.4 Log Monitoring
The package also contains log-monitoring utilities that infer progress and estimated remaining time by regular-expression matching against subprocess output. Those values are operational heuristics and may change if the upstream log format changes.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 9  MethylAlignmentQC
text:
9.5 Publication Guidance
In a publication, methylalignmentqc should be described as:

a QC ingestion and normalization layer,
dependent on upstream Picard or Parabricks metrics,
deterministic in its parsing logic, and
not responsible for new statistical inference.

That framing keeps the package in scope without attributing more theory to it than the code actually implements.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
text:
10.1 Why This Chapter Exists
The repository is scientifically useful, but it is not served well by a perfectly tidy story. The code mixes exact formulas, approximations, heuristics, and external-service calls. This chapter records the main caveats that should be understood before publishing claims based on the pipeline.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
section: 10.2 The “ECDF-Only Pipeline” Claim Is Too Broad
text:
10.2 The “ECDF-Only Pipeline” Claim Is Too Broad
The centroid-detector-classifier path is indeed ECDF-centered. However:

methylmapper uses weighted Stouffer aggregation and heuristic importance scores,
methylenricher uses external enrichment plus heuristic module scoring,
methylalignmentqc is deterministic QC parsing, not ECDF inference.

Therefore the monorepo as a whole should not be marketed as purely ECDF-only. The safer statement is that the core supervised detection and classification path is ECDF-centered.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
text:
10.3 Dependence Is Real
Several methods rely on assumptions that are standard but imperfect for methylation data:

loci within one chromosome are correlated,
mapped DMPs within one gene are correlated,
binary OvR heads are not guaranteed to be jointly compatible,
repeated validation splits are not independent external studies.

This does not invalidate the workflow, but it does change how literally one should interpret p-values, q-values, and meta-analytic combinations.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
text:
10.4 Approximation Layers
The code intentionally trades exact raw-data procedures for scalable summaries:

KS statistics are evaluated on a grid and calibrated asymptotically,
Mann-Whitney is reconstructed from histograms rather than raw ranks,
ECDF overlap is integrated numerically after spline reconstruction,
some distance calculations average only over pairwise-overlapping loci.

These approximations should be reported as approximations, not hidden behind textbook method names alone.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
text:
10.5 Heuristic Layers
The following components are best described as engineering decisions:

the canonical effect-size ranking,
cumulative effect-mass selection,
geometric-mean control aggregation for pairwise OvR bundles,
module scoring constants in methylenricher,
stability thresholds for choosing top DMP counts in methylmapper,
auto-cap rules for coverage trimming.

These are often useful, but their outputs are not calibrated probabilities or test statistics.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
text:
10.6 External Dependencies
Some results depend on systems whose internal logic is not fully versioned inside this repository:

Enrichr,
DisGeNET,
Open Targets,
Azure SQL stored procedures,
optional Grok/xAI-assisted evidence synthesis.

Any publication using those layers should record service versions, access dates, and cache policies. Otherwise the results are reproducible only in a weak operational sense.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
text:
10.7 Legacy Or Experimental Remnants
The repository still contains legacy components, but their status is now clearer:

packages/methylutils/comparison.py contains a beta-based comparator path that is not used by the active detector/classifier production flow.
A few package-local docs can lag behind code evolution between releases.

To avoid methodological confusion, interpret these as historical/auxiliary artifacts, not active runtime estimators.

10.7.1 Current safeguards
The current docs/code governance already reduces this risk:

The Quarto theory book (docs/theory) is the canonical method reference.
Production workflow chapters describe the active ECDF-first detector/classifier path and the current model backends explicitly.
Legacy modules remain in-repo for compatibility and experimentation, but publication claims should cite only methods documented as active in this book.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
text:
10.8 Publication-Ready Positioning
The strongest defensible manuscript framing is:

the core pipeline summarizes methylation into centroids with empirical distributions,
it detects DMPs with nonparametric, ECDF-based screening and FDR adjustment,
it classifies samples with weighted empirical-distribution likelihoods,
and it layers biological annotation and pathway-level interpretation on top.

Anything stronger than that risks overstating what the code actually does.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 10  Limitations and Open Questions
section: 10.9 What Would Strengthen The Theory Further
text:
10.9 What Would Strengthen The Theory Further
The current implementation could support stronger future papers if the repository adds:

finite-sample benchmarking of histogram-based Mann-Whitney against raw-rank Mann-Whitney,
calibration studies for the effective-temperature ECDF classifier,
dependence-aware gene aggregation,
more explicit modeling of multiclass consistency,
and clearer retirement or isolation of legacy experimental branches.

Those are natural next steps, but they are not yet the state of the codebase.
crumbs: Part I: Mathematical and Statistical Foundations

title: 11  The Project Configuration File
text:
11.1 Role and Design Principle
MethylPipeline is controlled by a single JSON configuration file called the project configuration file (usually named project_<name>.json). Every pipeline step — centroid construction, DMP detection, classification, mapping, enrichment, prediction, and Monte Carlo validation — derives its inputs, outputs, and parameters from this one file.
The governing design principle is single source of truth: no piece of information that is already in the project file should be repeated inside any step-specific configuration. Specifically:
The Pydantic model that validates the project file is ProjectConfig in packages/methylutils/methyl_utils/pipeline_config.py.

text:
Sample paths are defined once in the top-level controls/diseases block and never duplicated in step_config.predictor.
output_base and samples_base_path are top-level fields inherited by all steps.
Monte Carlo validation settings are embedded under step_config.validation, not in a separate file.

title: 11  The Project Configuration File

text:
11.6 Embedding Monte Carlo Settings: step_config.validation
Rather than maintaining a separate monte_carlo_config.json file, the Monte Carlo validation settings can be embedded directly inside the project file under step_config.validation. When methyl-validation is invoked with --project <path>, it reads the step_config.validation block and constructs a MonteCarloConfig from it, inheriting samples_base_path, output_base, and the cohort structure from the top-level project fields.
The fields that are appropriate for step_config.validation are only the Monte Carlo-specific ones:
"validation": {
  "train_fraction": 0.8,
  "n_iterations": 50,
  "seed": 42,
  "run_stability": true,
  "stability_dmp_freq": 0.7,
  "stability_min_balanced_accuracy": 0.6,
  "abort_on_step_failure": false
}
Fields that are not needed here (because they are inherited from the project): samples_base_path, output_base, base_project, cohorts, healthy_csv, disease_csv.

11.6.1 Modeling backend inside step_config.validation
The same validation block also controls what happens during methyl-validation --model. The default backend is ecdf (classifier + predictor), but the project may select:

model_backend: "tabular_sklearn" for tabular bundle-based training/evaluation,
model_backend: "generative_hybrid" for the hybrid latent-density generative backend.

This keeps backend choice versioned in the same project JSON used for stability/freeze/model orchestration.

12.1 Overview
MethylPipeline supports two primary end-to-end operational workflows. They are designed to be run sequentially: Workflow 1 produces the final production model; Workflow 2 evaluates that model on random holdouts.
Both workflows are controlled entirely by the project configuration file and the step_config.validation embedded settings (see Chapter 11).
